protections: P1: a mount denied by view-level auth (login_required / permission_required / check_permissions) or by an on_mount hook must not leave a live event-dispatch channel: the WebSocket is closed (the sibling PermissionDenied branch closes 4403) or the view is unmounted, so post-denial frames cannot reach an @event_handler (websocket.py:1976-1978, 1979-1986, 2005-2007; event gate websocket.py:2722-2724).

P2 (must-keep-working): a denial inside a multiplexed mount_batch must NOT terminate the shared socket - the redirect is reported in the batch's navigate[] array and sibling views keep serving events (websocket.py:2524-2537, 2571-2596, 2671-2679; contract test test_wire_protocol_snapshots.py:249-262; client 03-websocket.js:529-539).
P3: every transport that implements mount must apply the same deny -> teardown rule; the SSE mount is a second hand-written implementation of the same operation (sse.py:155-246).

P4: an event must be authorized on the dispatch, not only at mount, for a session whose auth posture changed after the mount (websocket.py:2722-2724; websocket_utils.py:200-291 covers handler- and object-level only; docs/guides/authentication.md:197-206 calls mount-only auth a deliberate trade-off).
P5: a redirect target produced by developer hooks must be validated same-origin before it is sent to the client (mixins/request.py:84-99 does this for the HTTP path).

masking: The T1 fix cannot simply close: inside mount_batch (T3) the close is suppressed so sibling views survive, which leaves the batch-mounted denied view still installed on the consumer unless it is explicitly cleared; the suppression hides the residual exposure behind a passing batch response.

In the SSE mount, T4 is reachable only because view_instance is assigned before the auth check (sse.py:229); fixing only the redirect branch still leaves the PermissionDenied branch (sse.py:238-240) and the fail-open exception path (sse.py:245-246) dispatching, so the sibling branches mask each other.

conflicts.what: The natural fix for T1/T2 - an unconditional await self.close(code=4403) in the redirect branch - kills a multiplexed mount_batch: _mount_one swaps only send_json (websocket.py:2524-2527), the batch response carrying navigate[] is sent after the loop (2671-2679), and the client turns batch navigate entries into a live_redirect on that same socket (03-websocket.js:529-539, pinned by test_wire_protocol_snapshots.py:249-262).

The same close applied on the handle_live_redirect_mount entry (websocket.py:4290-4291) terminates an already-open SPA session on a mid-session login redirect, so the fix must distinguish a first mount from a re-mount on an open socket instead of closing blindly.

fairness_risks: A blanket 'any mount denial closes the socket' rule contradicts the mount_batch contract that a redirect must be reported in navigate[] while the socket keeps serving sibling views (websocket.py:2671-2679, test_wire_protocol_snapshots.py:249-262, 03-websocket.js:529-539).

The WebSocket client has no 'navigate' case (03-websocket.js:303-975; only 03b-sse.js:270-273 handles it), so a rule that accepts 'send navigate and return' as the fix would keep the broken behaviour; the graded behaviour has to be socket termination or unmount, not the frame.

A per-event view-level re-check (T6) contradicts the documented trade-off at docs/guides/authentication.md:197-206 and costs a query per interaction; if graded, a documented legitimate design is called a regression.

Closing on a redirect during handle_live_redirect_mount refuses a shape a legitimate SPA navigation needs (a user whose login expired mid-navigation must be able to log in and return), so 'close on every redirect' is too broad.

'Legacy' is not the same as unused for SSE: DjustSSEStreamView.get (?view=) is the mount the current SSE client still uses (03b-sse.js:51-59, sse.py:730), so a rule that simply disables that endpoint breaks the shipped fallback transport.

If the per-event re-check is added, views whose handlers were written against mount-only auth (docs/guides/authentication.md:195-206) start erroring after logout; the refused shape (events after revocation) is exactly the shape the documented design permits.

design.why: T1/T2 give the report-described base (a redirect exit that leaves a live channel, on both the auth and the on_mount producer, plus the live_redirect_mount re-entry) and are cheap for both models. T3 is the MiMo-shaped trap: the obvious close breaks a pinned, client-consumed batch contract, so the solver must suppress the close in the batch path AND still clear the denied view from the single view_instance slot. T4 is the DeepSeek-shaped trap: a second, hand-written mount implementation in another module whose docstring claims the same security model, with a real reason to dismiss it as the degraded fallback transport. T5 rides along in T4's fix site. That is three independent groups with three different reasons to dismiss (batch contract, developer-hook semantics, legacy fallback transport), one deepseek-type and one mimo-type. T6 (per-event re-auth) would be a strong fourth group and the hardest deepseek-type, but only if graders accept it as in scope; T7 (hook-redirect host validation) is real and evidence-backed but a different protection class (CWE-601) and is left out of the design.
